name: Energy and Change
what_is_it: Energy and Change studies different forms of energy, how energy transfers and transforms from one form to another, and how electric circuits work.
why_it_matters: Every device you use — a phone, a kettle, a light bulb — relies on energy transformation and electric circuits. Understanding this helps explain how electricity is generated, distributed, and used safely.
key_vocabulary: Energy — the ability to do work or cause change; it cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed
Kinetic energy — the energy of motion
Potential energy — stored energy due to position or condition (e.g. a stretched spring, water behind a dam)
Electric circuit — a closed loop through which electric current can flow
Current — the flow of electric charge through a conductor
Conductor — a material that allows electric current to flow easily (e.g. copper)
Insulator — a material that does not allow electric current to flow easily (e.g. rubber, plastic)
Series circuit — a circuit with only one path for current to flow
Parallel circuit — a circuit with more than one path for current to flow
core_concept: Energy is never lost — it just changes form (this is the Law of Conservation of Energy). In a circuit, a power source (like a battery) pushes electric charge around a closed loop, and that electrical energy transforms into other forms (light, heat, sound, movement) at each component.
key_facts: A complete, unbroken circuit is required for current to flow — any break stops the whole circuit.
In a series circuit, if one component fails, the whole circuit stops working because there's only one path.
In a parallel circuit, other branches keep working even if one branch fails, because current has alternative paths.
A battery converts stored chemical energy into electrical energy.
A light bulb converts electrical energy into light energy AND heat energy (some energy is always 'lost' as heat).
common_misconceptions: Thinking a battery 'stores electricity' — it actually stores chemical energy that gets converted to electrical energy when connected.
Believing current is 'used up' as it flows around a circuit — the same current flows throughout a series circuit; energy is transferred, not the current itself consumed.
Assuming energy can be 'lost' completely — it's always transformed into another form (often heat), never destroyed.
Confusing series and parallel circuits — remember: series = one path, parallel = multiple paths.
